topic: Scope functions II: run, with, takeIf & choosing one

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `s.run { ... }` makes `s` the receiver (`this`) and returns the lambda's last expression. `length + 1` is `6 + 1`, so `r` is `7`, not the string itself.

questions.question: Which statement about `with(obj) { ... }` is true?
options: It is a plain function that takes `obj` as an argument, exposes it as `this` and returns the lambda result
It is an extension function on `obj` that exposes it as `it` and returns the lambda result
It is a plain function that takes `obj` as an argument, exposes it as `this` and returns the receiver `obj`
It is an extension function on `obj` that exposes it as `this` and returns `obj` itself
questions.explanation: `with` is declared as `fun <T, R> with(receiver: T, block: T.() -> R): R`. The object is passed as an argument (not a receiver of `with`), is `this` inside the block, and the block's result is returned. Returning the object itself is what `apply` does.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `takeIf` returns the receiver when the predicate is true and `null` otherwise. `7` is odd, so `a` is `null`; `8` passes, so `b` is `8`. It never returns the Boolean itself.

questions.question: Given `val user: User?`, you can write `user?.with { name }` so the block runs only when `user` is non-null.
questions.explanation: `with` is not an extension function, so there is nothing to call with `?.`; this doesn't compile. Use `user?.run { name }`, which is an extension and gives the same `this`-receiver, result-returning behaviour.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Inside `with(sb)`, `append` and `length` are called on `sb`. `with` returns the last expression, `length`, which is `3` after appending `"Hi"` and `"!"`. The builder itself still holds `Hi!`.

questions.question: Given `val user: User?`, which call runs the block only when `user` is non-null, with the non-null `user` as `this`?
questions.explanation: `?.run` skips the call entirely when `user` is null, and inside the block `this` is a non-null `User`. `with(user)` and `user.run` always run the block with a nullable `this`, so `name` would need `?.`, and the plain `run` block has no receiver at all.

questions.question: `run { ... }` called without a receiver is a non-extension function that simply executes the block and returns its result, which makes it handy for computing a value from a few temporary local variables.
questions.explanation: There are two `run`s: the extension `T.run { }` and the top-level `run { }`. The top-level one has no receiver; it just runs the block and returns its last expression, keeping helper variables scoped to the block.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The `x` declared inside the `run` block shadows the outer one only inside the block, so the block returns `3 * 2 = 6`. The outer `x` is untouched and still `10`.

questions.question: You need a scope function that exposes the object as `this`, returns the lambda result, and can be chained with `?.` on a nullable value. Which one fits?
questions.explanation: `run` is the extension counterpart of `with`: `this` receiver, returns the lambda result, and as an extension it works with `?.`. `with` can't be used with `?.`, `apply` returns the receiver, and `let` exposes the object as `it`.

questions.question: Which scope functions expose the context object as `this` (not `it`) inside the lambda?
questions.explanation: `run`, `with` and `apply` take a lambda with receiver (`T.() -> R`), so the object is `this`. `let` and `also` take a regular lambda (`(T) -> R`), so the object is the parameter `it`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `takeUnless` returns the receiver only when the predicate is false. The input is blank, so the predicate is true and the result is `null`, which the elvis replaces with `"Guest"`.

questions.question: In `onBindViewHolder(holder: ItemViewHolder, position: Int)`, `holder.binding` is a non-null view binding and you need to set `title`, `subtitle` and `avatar` from `item`. You don't need a return value. Which option is the idiomatic choice?
options: `holder.binding.takeIf { it != null }!!.run { title.text = item.name; subtitle.text = item.email; avatar.load(item.photo) }`
`holder.binding.let { it }.apply { title.text = item.name }.also { it.subtitle.text = item.email }.run { avatar.load(item.photo) }`
questions.explanation: `with` reads as "with this binding, do the following": it groups calls on a non-null object whose result you don't need. The `takeIf`/`!!` null check is pointless on a non-null value, the receiver-less `run` still repeats `holder.binding` everywhere, and chaining four scope functions only adds noise.

questions.question: A bare `return` inside `user.run { ... }` (in a regular function) leaves only the lambda, and execution continues with the next statement after `run`.
questions.explanation: Because `run` is inline, a bare `return` inside its lambda is a non-local return: it returns from the enclosing function. To leave only the lambda, use a labelled return such as `return@run value`.

questions.question: `val isValid = binding.run { email.text.isNotBlank() && password.text.length >= 8 }` makes `isValid` a `Boolean`. Which replacement keeps `isValid` a `Boolean` with the same body?
questions.explanation: `with(binding)` has the same `this` receiver and also returns the lambda result. `apply` and `also` return the binding itself, and `takeIf` returns the binding or `null` (its lambda also gets `it`, not `this`, so the body wouldn't even resolve `email`).

questions.question: Which statements about `takeIf` and `takeUnless` are true?
options: The return type is nullable (`T?`) even when `x` is non-null
`x.takeUnless { cond(it) }` gives the same result as `x.takeIf { !cond(it) }`
They are lazy: the predicate runs only if the result is later used
On a `List`, `takeIf` keeps only the elements that match, like `filter`
questions.explanation: Both return the receiver or `null`, so the type is always `T?`, and `takeUnless` is just the negated form. The predicate is evaluated immediately on every call, and on a `List` the predicate receives the whole list, not each element.

questions.question: What is the main problem with this code?
options: Each level rebinds `this` and `it`, so it's unclear whether `zip` is the address's or the view's
It doesn't compile, because `with` can't be nested inside another lambda with receiver
It is slow, because each of the four scope functions allocates a new lambda object on every call
`also` can't be called on a `String`, so the `city?.also` line fails to compile
questions.explanation: Nesting scope functions stacks implicit receivers: inside `with(view)`, an unqualified `zip` resolves to `view.zip` if it exists, otherwise to `address.zip`, and readers can't tell which. The code does compile, `also` works on any type, and these inline functions don't allocate lambdas. Flatten it with early returns and named `val`s.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `return@run "blank"` only leaves the lambda, so `r` becomes `blank`. The bare `return "long"` is a non-local return from `check` itself, so `r=` is never prepended. For `null`, `?.run` is skipped and the elvis gives `none`.

questions.question: What happens with this code in a Fragment factory?
options: Compile error: `with` returns the lambda result, `Unit` here, not a `Bundle`
It works: `with` returns the `Bundle` after running the block
It compiles, but `arguments` ends up as an empty `Bundle`
It compiles, but throws a `NullPointerException` when the fragment reads its arguments
questions.explanation: `with` returns the last expression, and `putInt` returns `Unit`, so `args` is `Unit` and assigning it to `arguments` is a type mismatch. Use `Bundle().apply { ... }` to get the configured `Bundle` back.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Inside `child?.run`, the nearest receiver is the child, so `name` is `kid`. `this@with.name` explicitly reaches the outer receiver, `root`. Needing labels like this is a sign the nesting is hurting readability.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `s?.takeIf` is skipped because `s` is null, so its predicate never runs. `s.takeIf` is called on `String?` directly, so its predicate always runs (logging `b`); it is true, and `takeIf` returns the receiver, which is `null`.
